lessons.sub: Why security people use Python, and how to run it.
learn: Why Python
Python is the most common scripting language in security. Analysts use it to parse logs, call APIs, automate checks and glue tools together. Kali already has Python 3 installed.
Two ways to run it
Type `python3` to open the interactive prompt and try lines one at a time. Or save code in a file ending in .py and run `python3 hello.py`. Leave the prompt with `exit()`.
print and comments
`print()` shows output. Anything after `#` is a comment that Python ignores. Use comments to explain why, not what.

# Say hello to the SOC
print("Hello, SOC")
print(2 + 3)
Indentation is syntax
Python groups code by indentation, not braces. Lines inside an if or a loop are indented, usually by four spaces. What Python requires is consistency; getting it wrong is an error, not a style issue.
real: On the job
A SOC analyst gets 2,000 alerts exported to a file. Reading them by hand takes a day. A 15-line script sorts and counts them in a second. That's why so many security job ads mention Python.
myth: You have to be a programmer to use Python in security.
Most security scripts are short: read something, filter it, count it, print it. You'll write useful ones by the end of this track.

tryit.p: Create a file, run it, then change the message and run it again.
tryit.code:
echo 'print("Hello from Kali")' > hello.py
python3 hello.py

quiz.w: The second line is a comment, so only `print(2 + 3)` runs.

quiz.q: How do you run a script saved as scan.py?
quiz.w: Give the file to the python3 interpreter.

quiz.q: What happens when you run this?
quiz.w: The body of an if must be indented. Python refuses to run the file.

recap: Python is the security team's glue language.

lessons.sub: Names for values, and why text isn't a number.
learn: Variables
A variable is a name for a value. You create one by assigning to it with `=`. Pick names that say what the value is, like `target_ip`, not `x`.

target_ip = "10.10.10.20"
port = 445
print(target_ip, port)
The core types
`str` is text, `int` is a whole number, `float` has a decimal point and `bool` is True or False. `type()` tells you which one you have.
Text isn't a number
Anything you read from a file, a log or user input arrives as text. "22" + "1" joins text into "221"; it doesn't add. Convert with `int()` before doing maths.
Converting
`int("22")` turns text into a number and `str(22)` turns a number into text. Converting text that isn't a number, like `int("ssh")`, raises a ValueError.
real: On the job

A firewall export lists ports as text. A script that checks `"80" > "443"` says True, because text compares character by character and 8 beats 4. As numbers, 80 > 443 is False. Converting to int first fixes it.
myth: Python works out what you meant, so types don't matter.
Python won't guess. Mixing text and numbers either raises an error or quietly does the wrong thing.

tryit.p: Type each line into the Python prompt and predict the result before you press Enter.

quiz.w: Both values are text, so `+` joins them.
`int()` converts the text to a number first, so this is real addition.
The decimal point makes it a float, even though the value is a whole number.

recap: Assign with `=`, and use descriptive names.
str, int, float and bool are the core types.
Input from files and logs is text.

learn: String methods
Strings come with built-in methods. `.lower()` and `.upper()` change case, `.strip()` removes spaces and newlines from the ends, and `.replace()` swaps text.

user = "  Admin \n"
print(user.strip().lower())
Split into parts
`.split()` breaks a string into a list of words. With an argument it splits on that character instead. It's the quickest way to pull fields out of a log line.

line = "Failed password for root from 10.0.0.5"
parts = line.split()
print(parts[-1])
Searching
`in` checks whether text appears anywhere in a string. `.startswith()` and `.endswith()` check the ends. All of them are case-sensitive.
f-strings
Put an f before the quotes and you can drop variables straight into text with braces. They're the clearest way to build output and messages.

ip = "10.10.10.20"
open_ports = 3
print(f"{ip} has {open_ports} open ports")
real: On the job
Phishing triage often starts with string checks: does the sender's domain end with your company's domain, or with a look-alike? A couple of `.endswith()` and `.lower()` calls handle that.
myth: `in` and `==` do the same thing.
`==` needs an exact match. `in` finds text anywhere, so "admin" in "sysadmin" is True. That difference causes real filtering bugs.

tryit.h: Pull fields from a log line
tryit.p: Split a real-looking SSH log line and print the user and IP address.
tryit.code:
line = "Failed password for invalid user test from 10.10.10.10 port 51234 ssh2"
parts = line.split()
print("user:", parts[5])
print("ip:", parts[7])

quiz.w: Counting starts at 0: Failed is 0, password is 1, for is 2.
`in` matches anywhere inside the string, which is easy to forget when filtering usernames.
The f prefix fills in the braces with the variable's value.

recap: `in` matches anywhere; `==` needs an exact match.
Indexes start at 0, and -1 is the last item.

lessons.sub: Doing the same thing to many items.
learn: Lists
A list holds items in order, in square brackets. Get an item by its index, starting at 0. `len()` gives the number of items and `.append()` adds one to the end.

ports = [22, 80, 443]
ports.append(3389)
print(ports[0], len(ports))
for loops
A for loop runs its indented block once for each item. This is how you check every host, every port or every log line.

for port in [22, 80, 443]:
    print("checking", port)
range
`range(1, 5)` produces 1, 2, 3 and 4. The end number is not included. It's handy for port ranges and counting.
Filtering as you go
Combine a loop and an if to keep only what matters. Build a new list of matches, then work with that.
real: On the job
A vulnerability scanner returns 500 findings. A loop that keeps only the critical ones on internet-facing hosts gives you a short list to fix first.
myth: `range(1, 5)` includes 5.
The stop value is excluded, so `range(1, 5)` gives 1 to 4. For ports 1 to 1024, write `range(1, 1025)`.

tryit.p: Loop over your lab addresses and print a line for each. Then change it to skip the Kali address.

quiz.w: Index 1 is the second item, because counting starts at 0.
The start is included and the stop is not.

quiz.code:
total = 0
for n in [3, 4, 5]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
quiz.w: The loop adds each number to the running total: 3, then 7, then 12.

recap: Lists hold ordered items; indexes start at 0.
for loops run once per item.
Loop plus if filters a list.

lessons.sub: Look things up by name, and count what you see.
learn: Dictionaries
A dictionary maps keys to values, in curly braces. Look a value up by its key, the way DNS looks up an address by name.

services = {22: "ssh", 80: "http", 443: "https"}
print(services[443])
Safe lookups
Looking up a missing key with square brackets raises a KeyError. `.get(key, default)` returns the default instead, which is safer with messy data.
Counting by hand
To count things, add 1 to a dictionary value each time you see a key. Start missing keys at 0 with `.get()`.
Counter does it for you
`collections.Counter` counts a list in one line, and `.most_common(n)` gives the top n. It's perfect for top talkers and top failed-login sources.

from collections import Counter
fails = ["1.1.1.1", "2.2.2.2", "1.1.1.1"]
print(Counter(fails).most_common(1))
real: On the job
“Which IPs failed to log in the most last night?” is a daily SOC question. Read the log, pull out the IPs, put them in a Counter, print `most_common(10)`. Done.
myth: Dictionaries are only for advanced code.
They're one of the most useful beginner tools: look-up tables, counts and parsed JSON are all dictionaries.

tryit.p: Count how often each IP appears and print the top two.
tryit.code:
from collections import Counter
ips = ["10.10.10.20", "10.10.10.30", "10.10.10.20", "8.8.8.8", "10.10.10.20"]
for ip, n in Counter(ips).most_common(2):
    print(ip, n)

quiz.w: 443 isn't a key, so `.get()` returns the default you gave it.
`most_common` returns a list of (item, count) pairs, highest first.

o: The first time an IP appears it isn't a key yet
quiz.w: Square brackets on a missing key raise a KeyError. `.get` starts new keys at 0.

lessons.sub: Make decisions, then package code you'll reuse.
learn: if, elif, else
An if runs its block only when the condition is true. elif checks the next condition and else catches everything left. Only the first matching branch runs.
Comparisons
`==` means equal and `!=` means not equal. `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare numbers. Combine conditions with `and`, `or` and `not`. A single `=` assigns; it never compares.
Functions
`def` defines a function: a named block you can call again and again. Parameters go in the brackets, and `return` sends a result back.
Why functions matter
Functions stop you copying code around. Fix a bug once and every caller gets the fix. They also make scripts easier to test and read.
real: On the job
Detection rules are functions in disguise: given an event, return True if it's suspicious. Writing small functions like `is_off_hours(timestamp)` is exactly how SIEM and SOAR logic is built.
myth: A function that prints a result returns it too.
print shows a value on screen; return hands it back to the caller. A function without return gives back None.

tryit.p: Write a function that flags a login as suspicious after more than five failures, then test it with a few values.

quiz.w: 3 isn't over 10 or over 5, so neither the if nor the elif runs, and the else branch prints ok.
The function multiplies its two arguments and returns 12.

quiz.code:
def check(port):
    print("checked", port)

result = check(22)
print(result)
quiz.w: The function prints but never returns, so `result` is None.

recap: if, elif and else choose a branch.
`def` packages code; `return` hands back a result.
Small functions make detection logic readable.

learn: Open with with
`with open(path) as f:` opens a file and closes it automatically when the block ends, even if an error happens. Use it every time.
Line by line
Looping over a file gives one line at a time, so even a huge log fits in memory. Each line ends with a newline, which `.strip()` removes.
Writing files
Open with "w" to write a new file, which replaces anything already there. Use "a" to append. Writing your results to a file makes them easy to attach to a ticket.
Messy logs
Real logs contain odd characters. `open(path, errors="replace")` swaps unreadable bytes for a placeholder instead of crashing halfway through.
real: On the job

An incident responder receives a 2 GB web server log. Opening it in Notepad hangs the laptop. A Python loop reads it line by line, keeps only requests from the suspect IP and writes them to a small file.
myth: You must load the whole file before searching it.
Looping over the file object reads one line at a time. That's faster to start and works on files bigger than your RAM.

tryit.p: SSH isn't running on Kali by default. Start it, fail a login, export the log, then count the failures with Python.
tryit.code:
sudo systemctl start ssh
ssh nobody@localhost    # type yes, a wrong password, then Ctrl+C
sudo journalctl -u ssh > ssh.log
python3 -c '
count = 0
with open("ssh.log", errors="replace") as f:
    for line in f:
        if "Failed password" in line:
            count += 1
print(count, "failed logins")
'
sudo systemctl stop ssh

quiz.q: What does `with open(...) as f:` give you that plain `open()` doesn't?
o: The file closes automatically when the block ends
quiz.w: The with block guarantees the file is closed, even if an error interrupts it.

quiz.q: You open report.txt with mode "w". What happens to what was already in it?
o: New text is added to the end
quiz.w: "w" truncates the file. Use "a" to append instead.

quiz.q: Why loop over a log file line by line instead of reading it all at once?
o: It handles files bigger than memory
quiz.w: Only one line is held at a time, so file size stops mattering.

recap: Loop over the file to read line by line.

lessons.sub: Find patterns, not just fixed text.
learn: What regex is
A regular expression is a pattern that matches text. Python's `re` module uses it to find IP addresses, usernames or error codes inside messy lines. Write patterns as raw strings, like `r"..."`.
Building blocks
`\d` matches a digit and `\S` any non-whitespace character. `+` means one or more. `.` matches any character, so escape it as `\.` when you mean a real dot.
Capture groups
Brackets capture part of a match. `re.search` returns a match object, and `.group(1)` gives you what the first brackets captured.

import re
line = "Failed password for root from 10.0.0.5 port 22"
m = re.search(r"from (\S+)", line)
if m:
    print(m.group(1))
findall
`re.findall` returns every match in the text as a list. It's the quickest way to pull all the IP addresses or numbers out of a line.
real: On the job
Threat intel reports list indicators like IPs and domains buried in paragraphs. A regex pulls them out in seconds so they can be blocked or searched for in your SIEM.
myth: You need to memorise regex syntax.
Nobody does. Learn the few building blocks here, then test patterns on a site like regex101 or in the Python prompt.

tryit.p: Pull every IPv4-looking address out of a block of text. The pattern is simple, so it can match impossible values like 999.1.1.1; real tools also validate.
tryit.code:
import re
text = "Blocked 10.10.10.10 and 203.0.113.7; allowed 10.10.10.20"
print(re.findall(r"\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+", text))

quiz.code:
import re
m = re.search(r"from (\S+)", "Failed password for root from 10.0.0.5 port 22")
print(m.group(1))
quiz.w: The brackets capture the non-space text right after "from ".
findall returns every match as a string inside a list.

quiz.q: Why write the pattern as `r"\d+"` instead of `"\d+"`?
o: The r keeps backslashes exactly as typed
quiz.w: A raw string stops Python treating backslashes as its own escapes. Without it, `\b` (a regex word boundary) silently becomes a backspace character.

recap: `re.search` finds the first match; `re.findall` finds them all.
Capture groups pull out just the part you need.

lessons.sub: Fingerprints, file checks and why Base64 isn't security.
learn: hashlib
Python's `hashlib` computes hashes like SHA-256. Hash functions work on bytes, so encode text first with `.encode()`. `.hexdigest()` gives the familiar hex string.

import hashlib
print(hashlib.sha256("hello".encode()).hexdigest())
Hashing a file
Read the file in binary mode and feed it to the hash in chunks, so large files don't fill memory. Compare the result with the publisher's hash to check integrity.
Encoding isn't encryption
Base64 turns bytes into safe text for email or URLs. Anyone can reverse it with no key. Seeing Base64 in a script or config means obscured, not protected.
Passwords need more
SHA-256 is too fast for storing passwords. Use a slow, salted algorithm such as Argon2 or bcrypt, through a library like argon2-cffi. Never write your own.
real: On the job
Malware analysts share file hashes, not files. Searching a SHA-256 in a threat intel service tells you in seconds whether a suspicious attachment is already known to be malicious.
myth: Base64 hides secrets.
Base64 is encoding: one line of Python reverses it. Attackers use it to dodge simple text filters, not to protect anything.

tryit.p: Hash any file and compare the result with `sha256sum` on the same file. They should match exactly.
tryit.code:
import hashlib, sys
h = hashlib.sha256()
with open(sys.argv[1], "rb") as f:
    for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
        h.update(chunk)
print(h.hexdigest())
# run: python3 hashfile.py /etc/hostname
# compare: sha256sum /etc/hostname

quiz.w: SHA-256 is 256 bits, which is 32 bytes, which is 64 hex characters.

o: An error, because you need a key
quiz.w: No key needed. That's why Base64 is encoding, not encryption.

quiz.q: Which should you use to store user passwords?
quiz.w: Password hashes must be slow and salted so stolen hashes are expensive to crack.

recap: Hash big files in chunks, in binary mode.

lessons.sub: Talk to the network directly, in your lab only.
learn: The socket module
A socket is one end of a network connection. `socket.socket()` makes a TCP socket, and `connect_ex((host, port))` tries to connect. It returns 0 when the port is open.
Always set a timeout
Without a timeout, a filtered port can hang your script for a long time. `s.settimeout(1)` gives up after a second. Close each socket when you're done with it.
A tiny port check
Loop over a few ports and report the open ones. This is a TCP connect check: the full handshake completes, unlike Nmap's SYN scan.

import socket
host = "10.10.10.20"
for port in [22, 135, 445, 3389]:
    s = socket.socket()
    s.settimeout(1)
    if s.connect_ex((host, port)) == 0:
        print(port, "open")
    s.close()
Permission still applies
A Python scanner is still a scanner. Only point it at systems you own or have written permission to test. Your internal lab is fine.
real: On the job

Tools like Nmap are better for real scanning. But a 10-line socket check is perfect inside automation, for example confirming a service came back up after a patch or that a port is closed after a firewall change.
myth: Writing your own scanner makes you stealthier than Nmap.
A connect scan completes the handshake, so it's noisier than a SYN scan and easily logged. Use Python for automation, not stealth.

tryit.p: Save the learn card's code as portcheck.py and run it. Then compare the result with `sudo nmap -sS -p 22,135,445,3389 10.10.10.20`.

quiz.q: What does `connect_ex` return when a port is open?
quiz.w: It returns an error number, and 0 means no error: the connection succeeded.

o: So filtered ports don't hang the script
quiz.w: A firewall that silently drops packets never answers. The timeout stops your script waiting.

quiz.q: How does this Python check differ from `nmap -sS`?
o: It completes the full TCP handshake
quiz.w: connect_ex does a full connect. Nmap's -sS sends SYN and never completes the handshake.

recap: Always set a timeout and close sockets.
A connect check completes the handshake.

lessons.sub: Two everyday formats in security automation.
learn: The ipaddress module
`ipaddress` understands IPv4 and IPv6. It can tell you if an address is private and whether it sits inside a network, so you don't parse dots by hand.

import ipaddress
ip = ipaddress.ip_address("10.10.10.20")
print(ip.is_private, ip in ipaddress.ip_network("10.10.10.0/24"))
JSON
Most security APIs, SIEM exports and cloud logs use JSON. `json.loads()` turns JSON text into Python dictionaries and lists, and `json.dumps()` turns them back into text.
Reading nested data
Parsed JSON is just dictionaries and lists inside each other. Reach into it step by step with keys and indexes.

import json
alert = json.loads('{"rule": "brute force", "src": {"ip": "203.0.113.7"}, "count": 42}')
print(alert["src"]["ip"], alert["count"])
Pretty printing
`json.dumps(data, indent=2)` prints JSON with line breaks and indents, which makes a messy API response readable in seconds.
real: On the job
A SIEM exports 300 alerts as JSON. A script loads them, keeps the ones whose source IP isn't private, and prints a short list of external addresses to check against threat intel.
myth: JSON is a Python thing.
JSON is a language-neutral text format used everywhere on the web. Python just happens to map it neatly onto dictionaries and lists.

tryit.p: Load a small list of alerts and print only the ones from public addresses. Note that documentation ranges like 203.0.113.0/24 also count as private; `is_global` is the stricter test.

quiz.w: 8.8.8.8 is a public address, so it isn't private.
JSON numbers become Python ints, so you get 3, not text.

quiz.code:
import ipaddress
net = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.1.0/26")
print(ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.1.70") in net)
quiz.w: A /26 starting at .0 covers .0 to .63, so .70 is outside it.

recap: `ipaddress` handles private checks and subnet membership.
`json.loads` turns JSON text into Python data.
Reach into nested data one key at a time.

lessons.sub: Scripts that handle bad input and take options.
learn: Exceptions
When something goes wrong, Python raises an exception, like FileNotFoundError or ValueError. Unhandled, it stops the script with a traceback.
try and except
Wrap risky code in try, and handle a specific exception in except. Catch the errors you expect; a bare `except:` hides real bugs.
Fail safely
If a security check can't complete, decide what happens. A function that returns True for “allowed” when it hits an error is failing open, which is OWASP 2025 A10. Default to deny.
Command-line arguments
`argparse` turns `python3 tool.py ssh.log --threshold 5` into named values, with help text for free. It makes a script reusable without editing the code.

import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Count failed logins")
p.add_argument("logfile")
p.add_argument("--threshold", type=int, default=5)
args = p.parse_args()
print(args.logfile, args.threshold)
real: On the job
A scheduled script crashes at 3am because one log line is malformed, and nobody notices for a week. Handling the expected error, logging it and carrying on keeps monitoring alive.
myth: Catching every exception with a bare except is the safe choice.
It hides bugs and can even catch Ctrl+C. Catch the specific errors you expect and let real problems surface.

tryit.p: Run it with a file that exists, then with one that doesn't, and see the difference.
tryit.code:
import sys
try:
    with open(sys.argv[1]) as f:
        print(sum(1 for _ in f), "lines")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("No such file:", sys.argv[1])
    sys.exit(1)
# python3 safe_read.py /etc/hostname
# python3 safe_read.py nope.log

quiz.w: "8080" is all digits, so `int()` works, the print runs and the except block is skipped.

quiz.q: An access check hits a database error and returns True. What's wrong?
o: It fails open, so errors grant access
quiz.w: When a check can't finish, deny by default. Failing open turns an outage into a breach.

o: Named command-line options with built-in help
quiz.w: Users can change inputs without editing the code, and `--help` documents the options.

lessons.sub: Use Python to audit an AWS account.
learn: What boto3 is

boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python. On Kali, install it with `sudo apt install python3-boto3`, because plain pip is blocked outside a virtual environment. Cloud security teams use it to audit settings across many accounts and services.
Credentials
boto3 finds credentials from `aws configure`, environment variables or an IAM role. Never put access keys in your code. Use a read-only role for audits, following least privilege.
Asking AWS questions
A client object exposes API calls as methods. Responses are dictionaries, the same as parsed JSON.

import boto3
s3 = boto3.client("s3")
for b in s3.list_buckets()["Buckets"]:
    print(b["Name"])
Handle missing settings
Some calls raise ClientError when a setting doesn't exist, such as a bucket with no public access block. Check the error code, so a permissions problem isn't mistaken for a missing setting.
real: On the job

Misconfigured cloud storage is behind many data exposures, and it's OWASP 2025 A02. A short boto3 script that flags buckets without a public access block is a classic cloud security interview project.
myth: A script that finds no problems proves the account is safe.
It only checks what you wrote it to check. Account-level settings, bucket policies and ACLs all affect public access too. Treat scripts as one layer.

tryit.where: Your own AWS account, read-only role
tryit.p: New buckets have blocked public access by default since April 2023, so REVIEW usually means an older bucket. Account-level settings also apply. Use your own account, never an employer's without approval.
tryit.code:
import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError
s3 = boto3.client("s3")
for b in s3.list_buckets()["Buckets"]:
    name = b["Name"]
    try:
        cfg = s3.get_public_access_block(Bucket=name)
        ok = all(cfg["PublicAccessBlockConfiguration"].values())
    except ClientError as e:
        if e.response["Error"]["Code"] != "NoSuchPublicAccessBlockConfiguration":
            print("ERROR ", name, e.response["Error"]["Code"])
            continue
        ok = False
    print("OK    " if ok else "REVIEW", name)

quiz.q: Where should a boto3 script get its AWS credentials?
o: From aws configure, environment variables or an IAM role
Hard-coded at the top of the script
From a comment in the code
quiz.w: Hard-coded keys leak through repos and screenshots. Let boto3 find credentials outside the code.

quiz.q: Why give an audit script a read-only role?
o: If the script or key leaks, it can't change anything
quiz.w: Least privilege limits the damage from a compromised script or credential.

quiz.q: In the Try it script, what does a NoSuchPublicAccessBlockConfiguration error mean?
o: The bucket has no bucket-level public access block, so review it
quiz.w: No block at bucket level doesn't prove it's public, but it means you should check the account settings and bucket policy. Other codes, like AccessDenied, mean a permissions problem instead.

recap: boto3 is the AWS SDK for Python.
Credentials come from outside the code.
A clean script result is one layer, not proof.

lessons.sub: Put the whole track together in one tool.
learn: The goal
Read an SSH log, find failed logins, count them per source IP and print the IPs over a threshold. It uses files, regex, Counter, functions, error handling and argparse.
The plan
Break it into steps before writing code: get arguments, open the file safely, match each line, count, then report. Each step is a few lines you already know.
The core
The heart of the tool is a loop with a regex and a Counter.

import re
from collections import Counter
pattern = re.compile(r"Failed password .* from (\S+)")
counts = Counter()
for line in ["Failed password for root from 10.0.0.5 port 22 ssh2"]:
    m = pattern.search(line)
    if m:
        counts[m.group(1)] += 1
print(counts)
Make it yours
Once it works, extend it: add a `--top` option, flag failures followed by a success from the same IP, or output JSON for a SIEM. Then write it up on GitHub.
real: On the job
Interviewers love a small, working tool you can explain line by line. “I wrote a script that finds brute-force sources in SSH logs” shows Python, log analysis and security thinking at once.
myth: Portfolio projects have to be big to count.
A small tool with a clear README, sample output and an honest list of limitations beats an unfinished large one.

tryit.p: Start SSH, fail a few logins with `ssh nobody@localhost`, then run `sudo journalctl -u ssh > ssh.log` and `python3 bruteforce.py ssh.log --threshold 2`. Stop SSH afterwards.

quiz.q: Which part of the detector pulls the source IP out of each line?
quiz.w: `(\S+)` after "from " captures the IP, and `.group(1)` returns it.

quiz.q: Why compile the regex once with `re.compile` outside the loop?
o: It avoids re-processing the pattern on every line
quiz.w: Python caches patterns anyway, but compiling once is clearer and avoids repeated work on huge logs.

quiz.q: Which extension would best catch a successful brute-force attack?
o: Flag an IP with many failures followed by a success
quiz.w: Many failures then a success from the same source is a classic sign that a password was guessed.

recap: Plan the steps, then code each one.
Regex extracts, Counter counts, argparse configures.
Write it up on GitHub with sample output.
